Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Law 10/2010 of 28 April on the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing, particularly Articles 3, 4, 7, 8, 14 and 25; Royal Decree 304/2014 of 5 May approving the implementing regulation of Law 10/2010; Royal Decree 609/2023 of 11 July establishing the Central Register of Beneficial Ownership and approving its regulation; applicable EU AML directives as transposed into Spanish law; Companies Act approved by Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July; and Registry Regulations under Decree 1784/1996 of 19 July.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

A registered office in Spain is required and must permit receipt of legal and administrative notices. A serviced or virtual office may be acceptable for a holding, consulting or early administrative phase if the provider permits legal domicile, mail handling, identification of the tenant and access for authorities. It is not adequate as the sole operational site for high-precision manufacture of intraocular lenses. The company should maintain a genuine production, quality-control, storage and record-access location appropriate to Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, Spanish medical-device rules and AEMPS oversight. Manufacturing premises, quality systems, technical documentation, traceability and post-market surveillance must be operational before commercial production.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Provincial (Provincial Commercial Registry of the registered-office province); name certification issued by the Registro Mercantil Central; supervisory control by the Dirección General de los Registros y del Notariado (DGRN).

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, de 2 de julio (Ley de Sociedades de Capital – LSC): Título II, arts. 20–34 (incorporation, public deed, registration); arts. 54–58 (Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada); art. 4 (minimum capital EUR 3,000); arts. 62–63 (bank deposit certificate); Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (RD 1784/1996).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura Pública de Constitución (notarized public deed of incorporation) followed by mandatory inscription in the Registro Mercantil, which confers legal personality (art. 33 LSC).

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 35 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

EUR 3,000 minimum share capital, fully subscribed and fully paid up at formation (LSC art. 4); cash contributions deposited in a Spanish bank account and evidenced by a bank deposit certificate issued within two months before the deed (LSC arts. 62–63); in-kind contributions described and valued in the deed; no separate escrow account is required.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety clearance: compliance certificate with CTE DB-SI (fire protection, evacuation routes) plus periodic municipal fire inspection; structural and load-bearing inspection for lathe machines and cleanroom per municipal building code (ITE); occupational risk prevention plan under Ley 31/1995 with workplace clearance by the Inspección de Trabajo; cleanroom area classified per ISO 14644 if aseptic manufacturing of sterile IOLs is declared.

Paid-in capital rule: EUR 3,000 minimum share capital, fully subscribed and fully paid up at formation (LSC art. 4); cash contributions deposited in a Spanish bank account and evidenced by a bank deposit certificate issued within two months before the deed (LSC arts. 62–63); in-kind contributions described and valued in the deed; no separate escrow account is required.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT) – sede electrónica: https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

A foreign entity forming or acquiring a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) must obtain a Spanish tax identification number (NIF) for the company. Process: (1) Obtain a provisional NIF from the AEAT Central Registry of Foreign Taxpayers before formal incorporation or through the notary/Registro Mercantil filing; (2) After registration, the entity is issued the definitive NIF (letter and 8 digits). For VAT purposes, the entity must separately register for the Census VAT roll (Censo de Obligados Tributarios) using model 036/037, declaring commencement of activity in manufacturing under CNAE 3250. Non-resident directors and shareholders may require an NIF or NIE depending on the act performed. No minimum capital is required for an SL, but all contributions must be bank-certified. The registration application must include the intended economic activity, place of establishment, and expected export operations.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A foreign entity forming or acquiring a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) must obtain a Spanish tax identification number (NIF) for the company. Process: (1) Obtain a provisional NIF from the AEAT Central Registry of Foreign Taxpayers before formal incorporation or through the notary/Registro Mercantil filing; (2) After registration, the entity is issued the definitive NIF (letter and 8 digits). For VAT purposes, the entity must separately register for the Census VAT roll (Censo de Obligados Tributarios) using model 036/037, declaring commencement of activity in manufacturing under CNAE 3250. Non-resident directors and shareholders may require an NIF or NIE depending on the act performed. No minimum capital is required for an SL, but all contributions must be bank-certified. The registration application must include the intended economic activity, place of establishment, and expected export operations.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain generally does not permit U.S.-style check-the-box pass-through elections for SLs; the SL is a capital company subject to Corporate Income Tax (Impuesto sobre Sociedades) on worldwide income if managed from or incorporated under Spanish law. Relevant statutory elections: (a) the freedom to elect a fiscal year matching the calendar year under the Corporate Income Tax Law (Article 21 LIS) except for certain group entities; (b) the application of the consolidation regime for tax groups under article 58 and following of the LIS; (c) the EU Anti-Tax-Avoidance Directive / ATAD-mandated controlled-foreign-company rules and hybrid mismatch election disclosures under DAC6 for cross-border arrangements; (d) eligibility to elect the reduced effective tax rate under the Patent Box regime and partial exemption of intra-group dividends under the participation exemption regime. No hybrid-mismatch neutralization election beyond the statutory conflict rules is available.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

General regime: no registration threshold – any person carrying out a taxable economic activity in Spanish territory must register for VAT from the first taxable transaction. Intra-Community distance sales thresholds: EUR 10,000 for EU-wide distance sales triggers Spanish VAT registration unless the OSS regime is used. Manufacturers exporting intraocular acrylic lenses (ISIC 3250) normally must register for Spanish VAT immediately upon commencing operations. Exception: small businesses using the recargo de equivalencia or simplified scheme have specific annual volume thresholds, but these are not applicable to an SL-exporter under the general VAT regime.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods dispatched or transported outside the European Union (third-country exports) are subject to 0% VAT (exempt with credit, i.e., zero-rated) provided the following are met: (a) the goods are physically exported from Spain within the period defined by customs law; (b) the supplier is the exporter or acts as such; (c) the export is evidenced by a valid customs export declaration and transport documents; (d) the goods are sold to a customer outside the EU; (e) in the case of contract manufacturing for a third-country customer, the goods must leave the EU customs territory. Intra-Community triangular sales to EU customers may also qualify for zero-rating under the VAT Directive if the customer provides a valid EU VAT number and goods are transported between Member States. Intraocular acrylic lenses destined for surgical implantation are generally taxed as ordinary goods; no medical zero-rating is automatic without export evidence.

  • Customs Export Declaration (DUA – Documento Único Administrativo) with export customs entry and AEAT validation date
  • Bill of Lading / Air Waybill / CMR transport document proving actual dispatch from the EU
  • Commercial invoice issued in accordance with Spanish VAT regulations
  • Proof of payment and Inward Remittance Certificate (Certificado de Ingreso de Divisas) or equivalent SWIFT/Letter of Credit settlement evidence
  • Export license and health/technical sanctions evidence for medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745
  • Incoterms documentary evidence (e.g., CIP, CIF, FOB contract and insurance certificate where applicable)

Electronic invoicing (factura electrónica) is mandatory between businesses and with the public administration. For B2B transactions, the 'Ley Crea y Crece' (Law 18/2022) mandates structured electronic invoicing with a private digital platform; all invoices must be machine-readable using European standard EN 16931. The AEAT is progressively introducing the Veri*Factu system for invoice software, requiring certification of billing software and QR/XML submission of invoice facts to the tax authority. Large companies subject to the Immediate Supply of Information (SII) must report invoice data in near-real time using web services (API). Digital stamping or fiscal signature is required for invoices issued through certified Veri*Factu software. For exporters, all export invoices must be issued electronically and linked to the corresponding customs export documentation.

The AEAT Customs and Excise Audit and VAT audit services scrutinize export zero-rating claims through documentary verification and cross-border data analytics. If an export is found not to have left the EU, or if documentation is false, incomplete, or untimely, the exporter loses the zero-rating and becomes liable for 21% VAT on the supply price, plus late-payment interest. A fraudulent export zero-rating scheme triggers: (a) tax base adjustment and VAT assessment; (b) penalty of 50% to 150% of the VAT amount under article 191 of the General Tax Law, depending on concealment; (c) dual penalties for both failure to issue the DUA and false customs declarations; (d) criminal liability under the Spanish Criminal Code if tax loss exceeds EUR 120,000, with imprisonment of 1 to 5 years; (e) retroactive clawback up to 4 years (or longer but for gross negligence and fraudulent concealment the prescriptive period runs to 10 years in certain customs cases). The exporter must retain the full customs and transport bundle for at least 6 years, and in case of intra-group or related-party exports, the transfer pricing documentation must separately substantiate arm's-length consideration in addition to customs and VAT documentary requirements.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

The euro is fully convertible for all current and capital transactions. Spain imposes no general exchange controls; capital movements within the EU and with third countries are liberalised pursuant to TFEU Article 63. Profit remittance for foreign direct investors is unrestricted for EU/EEA owners; non-EU investors must comply with foreign investment screening Law 19/2003 (prior notification for investments exceeding EUR 500 million in strategic sectors or 10% voting in listed companies), which is a declarative and approval-for-official-control requirement, not a currency convertibility hurdle. An SL distributing profits must meet Spanish Corporate Law (Law of Capital Companies, Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010) formalities: approved annual accounts, auditor report (if required), and corporate resolution, then remit freely through bank with BOP code 3700.

Export proceeds surrender rules

No statutory surrender, conversion, or repatriation timeline applies to export proceeds in foreign currency in Spain. Exporters may hold accounts abroad or retain foreign currency in Spanish accounts without limitation. For trade statistics and tax purposes, all cross-border goods movements must be declared to the Tax Agency (AEAT) using the Intrastat/Customs declarations; a summary declaration on the Single Administrative Document (SAD) and the annual 'Declaración de Operaciones con Pagos Exteriores' (external payments statement) are required, but no forced conversion exists.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain), operating within the Eurosystem and European System of Central Banks; foreign exchange and capital movement oversight is jointly administered with the Secretaría de Estado de Comercio (Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business) under European capital movement law.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Feasibility Rating: Medium with significant regulatory restrictions. Spanish-licensed EMI institutions (or EU EMIs passported under PSD2) may open accounts remotely, provide SEPA transfers and EUR/USD/GBP multi-currency accounts, and offer competitive FX pricing. However, EMIs cannot provideLetter of Credit (import/export) facilities, documentary collections, or trade finance guarantees. For a high-risk medical device manufacturer requiring LCs and cross-border clearing, an EMI can serve as a secondary or payables rail, but a Tier-1 bank is mandatory for core treasury and trade. Non-EU EMIs without a Spanish branch or passport cannot operate.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Root cause: Underwriting red flag: Origin of initial capital injection from a Latin American buyer (e.g., Colombia, Peru, Mexico) with unclear source of wealth.

Defense evidence: Provide audited financial statements of the parent/benefactor, shareholders resolution for capital distribution, signed purchase or loan agreement, bank statements from originating bank, tax residency certificate of investor, and a detailed organisational chart with UBO declaration. Include commercial justification for the lens distribution contract and pricing evidence to align with transfer pricing rules.
Underwriting red flag: Medical device sector deemed high-risk due to public procurement corruption, bribery risk in public hospitals, or sanctions exposure in target markets (e.g., Latin America).

Root cause: Underwriting red flag: Medical device sector deemed high-risk due to public procurement corruption, bribery risk in public hospitals, or sanctions exposure in target markets (e.g., Latin America).

Defense evidence: Submit ISO 13485 certification, EU CE marking (MDR 2017/745), national health registry filings, export licences for each destination country, evidence of local medical device agent, anti-bribery / anti-corruption policy, and completed due diligence on all distributors (including UBO and sanctions screening). Provide a clean compliance declarationand signed distributors' commitment not to pay bribery.
Underwriting red flag: UBO tax residency in a non-transparent jurisdiction (e.g., low-tax state) leading to FEI/CRS concerns.

Root cause: Underwriting red flag: UBO tax residency in a non-transparent jurisdiction (e.g., low-tax state) leading to FEI/CRS concerns.

Defense evidence: Submit a valid tax residency certificate issued by the respective tax authority, CRS self-certification, FATCA status, and underlying business rationale. Include copy of the SL's corporate register deed showing the UBO's role, board resolution for treasury operations, and evidence of substance (office lease, employee payroll, Spanish social security filings).

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

For a foreign direct investment (e.g., parent company injects capital into the Spanish SL), routing is via a SWIFT MT103 wire transfer to the SL's IBAN (ES + 22 digits) at the Spanish bank. Payment purpose must be coded as 'Capital Injection' and, for cross-border from a non-EU country, the corresponding Bank of Spain BOP code (e.g., 3610 - direct investment in Spain via equity capital) must be provided. Prior to execution, the SL* has 30 calendar days to file the foreign investment declaration with the Trade Directorate (Form D-1A) if the investor acquires 10% or more of the registered equity. The bank may require a board resolution approving the capital increase, a notarial deed of the increase, corporate tax ID (CIF/NIF), and the UBO proof. For EU/EEA investors, a prior declaration is not required but a statistics filing is still due. For cash under EUR 10,000, a simplified SEPA transfer is possible; for larger amounts, SWIFT/CHAPS equivalent is mandatory.For distributor payments or supplier settlements, the principal rails are: (1) SWIFT MT103 direct for invoice payments (must include purchase order, invoice, and shipping documents for customs purposes; BOP purpose code 3300 for goods, 3400 for services). (2) Commercial Letters of Credit (L/C) issued via SWIFT MT700, subject to UCP600, for large purchases or to mitigate counterparty risk; Spanish banks typically require 100% collateral or an approved working capital line. (3) For intra-EU settlements, SEPA Credit Transfer (SCT) protocol with unique 'CAD' shown in the reference field. Exports to Latin America require montly statistical filing with the AEAT; any payment above EUR 10,000 triggers the 'Form S-1' obligation to report to Banco de España under law 10/2010. For USD settlements, Spanish banks use the Federal Reserve Fedwire/SWIFT network; a correspondent bank in USA (e.g., JPMorgan or Citi) is required. The SL should maintain USD and EUR accounts plus a CLS-generated FX contract to settle daily net positions.Plain-vanilla FX forwards (EUR/USD, EUR/GBP, EUR/CNY) with up to 12 months tenors and tenors renewed only through rollovers at the same bankNon-deliverable forwards (NDFs) on non-fully-convertible LATAM currencies (COP, PEN, ARS, BRL) executed with Spanish credit entities or international counterparties where deliverability barrier appliesFX currency swaps for a two-way interest/principal exchange (EUR against USD) for trade financing or long-term cash-flow matchingEuropean-style FX options (call/put) for hedging lens export pricing against adverse currency movement while preserving upside for competitive bid pricingCross-currency basis swaps to convert USD asset receivables into EUR without re-entering the spot market twiceMarket-approved commodity/price hedging does not apply; only pure FX instruments are permitted due to the treasury policy

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Feasibility Rating: Medium with significant regulatory restrictions. Spanish-licensed EMI institutions (or EU EMIs passported under PSD2) may open accounts remotely, provide SEPA transfers and EUR/USD/GBP multi-currency accounts, and offer competitive FX pricing. However, EMIs cannot provideLetter of Credit (import/export) facilities, documentary collections, or trade finance guarantees. For a high-risk medical device manufacturer requiring LCs and cross-border clearing, an EMI can serve as a secondary or payables rail, but a Tier-1 bank is mandatory for core treasury and trade. Non-EU EMIs without a Spanish branch or passport cannot operate.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% general rate for Spanish resident companies, including a Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada. Newly incorporated entities generally qualify for a 15% rate in the first profitable tax period and the following period, subject to statutory exclusions and eligibility conditions.

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding tax on dividends and other profit distributions to non-residents, subject to domestic exemptions and applicable tax treaties. A qualifying EU parent company may obtain a full exemption under the Parent-Subsidiary Directive implementation, generally requiring at least 10% direct ownership, a minimum holding period, subject-to-tax and legal-form conditions, and anti-abuse compliance. The domestic participation exemption for a Spanish corporate recipient may also apply subject to statutory conditions and a 5% taxation inclusion rule.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

The return is due within the 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the end of the tax year. For a calendar-year company closing on 31 December, the ordinary filing window is generally 1 to 25 July of the following year, subject to the applicable electronic-filing calendar.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Normally filed during the first 20 calendar days of April, October, and December. For large taxpayers or specific electronic-payment arrangements, the applicable filing calendar and payment mechanics must be checked separately.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Spain has no single universal transaction-value threshold that eliminates all transfer-pricing obligations. Local-file documentation is generally required for material related-party transactions, subject to statutory exemptions. A commonly applicable documentation exemption is an aggregate annual value not exceeding EUR 250,000 per related person or entity, measured by transaction type and subject to exclusions and conditions. Master-file obligations generally apply to Spanish entities or permanent establishments belonging to an international group, subject to statutory scope and exemptions. Country-by-country reporting generally applies to groups meeting the EUR 750 million consolidated-revenue threshold.

Economic substance scope: Spain has no separate regime formally titled Economic Substance Regulations equivalent to certain offshore jurisdictions. Substance is nevertheless decisive under Spanish and EU anti-abuse rules, including beneficial-ownership requirements, the principal-purpose test in treaties, the general anti-abuse rule, controlled foreign company rules, anti-hybrid rules, interest limitation rules, exit-tax rules, and EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive anti-abuse provisions. The SL should maintain Spanish decision-making, personnel, premises, manufacturing capability, quality systems, inventory controls, risk management, board records, and commercially substantiated functions for its intraocular-lens manufacturing activity. Conduit dividends, circular financing, unsupported royalties, and profit allocations inconsistent with functions and risks are high-risk positions.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax evasion and false tax reporting

Statutory sanction: Administrative tax sanctions may generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax, with interest and recovery costs. Serious tax fraud may constitute a criminal offense where statutory monetary and intent thresholds are met, with imprisonment generally ranging from one to five years and fines linked to the defrauded amount; aggravated cases may attract higher imprisonment and fines.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur civil liability for tax debts and sanctions where they caused, tolerated, or failed to prevent the breach, and may face criminal liability as perpetrators, accomplices, or cooperating officers. Courts may impose asset seizure, restitution, disqualification from management, and imprisonment. Travel bans are not an automatic tax sanction but may be ordered by a court in criminal proceedings where legally justified.
Value-added tax fraud and carousel arrangements

Statutory sanction: VAT repayment, assessment of unpaid VAT, interest, and administrative sanctions commonly calculated as a percentage of the improperly deducted or unpaid amount. Serious or organized fraud may result in criminal prosecution, imprisonment, fines, asset seizure, and business disqualification.

Director personal liability: Directors and financial officers may be personally liable where they knowingly participated in or authorized the scheme. Criminal courts may order restitution, confiscation, management disqualification, and imprisonment; travel restrictions depend on judicial orders.
Transfer-pricing manipulation

Statutory sanction: The tax authority may make a primary adjustment, impose secondary adjustments, deny deductions, assess withholding tax, and apply documentation and tax sanctions. Transfer-pricing penalties may be based on undisclosed or incorrectly documented data and may be accompanied by interest.

Director personal liability: Directors may face civil liability for intentional or negligent tax damage and criminal liability if the adjustment forms part of deliberate tax fraud. A corporate veil may be pierced only under applicable statutory or judicial doctrines; imprisonment is not automatic and requires criminal findings.
Shell company, conduit, and beneficial-ownership abuse

Statutory sanction: Treaty, EU, and domestic exemptions may be denied; withholding may be reassessed at domestic rates; deductions may be denied; anti-abuse provisions may apply; and interest and sanctions may follow. Sham transactions may generate criminal exposure where tax-fraud thresholds are met.

Director personal liability: Directors may be liable for knowingly implementing artificial arrangements and may face civil restitution, tax sanctions, asset seizure, disqualification, and criminal imprisonment if the conduct satisfies criminal tax or fraud offenses. Judicial travel restrictions may be imposed in appropriate criminal proceedings.
Anti-money laundering and terrorist-financing breach

Statutory sanction: Spanish AML breaches may attract substantial administrative fines, public censure, temporary prohibitions, and management disqualification. Serious money laundering or terrorist-financing conduct may lead to criminal fines, confiscation, corporate dissolution or suspension, and imprisonment.

Director personal liability: Directors, compliance officers, and authorized signatories may be personally liable for knowing participation, consent, or grossly negligent control failures. Courts may order restitution, confiscation, management disqualification, and imprisonment; travel bans may arise from judicial precautionary measures.
Medical-device licensing and product-compliance violation

Statutory sanction: Authorities may order corrective actions, product withdrawal or recall, suspension or closure of facilities, license restrictions, administrative fines, and liability for patient or customer damage. Serious harm, falsification, or knowingly unsafe products may lead to criminal prosecution.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur civil compensation liability and criminal liability for knowingly placing unsafe or non-compliant medical devices on the market. Courts may impose fines, imprisonment, disqualification, confiscation, and precautionary travel restrictions where legally justified.
Accounting and corporate-record falsification

Statutory sanction: Possible consequences include accounting corrections, tax reassessment, administrative penalties, civil claims, insolvency-related liability, and criminal sanctions for false accounting, corporate fraud, or creditor prejudice.

Director personal liability: Directors may face personal civil liability, insolvency clawback, disqualification from administration, restitution, asset seizure, and imprisonment where criminal elements are established.
Undeclared cross-border payments and withholding failure

Statutory sanction: The SL may owe the unwithheld tax, interest, reporting penalties, and sanctions. Treaty relief may be denied where residence certificates, beneficial ownership, holding periods, or anti-abuse evidence are deficient.

Director personal liability: Directors may be secondarily liable under Spanish tax-liability rules where they caused or failed to remedy the withholding breach. Deliberate concealment may create criminal tax exposure, with restitution, fines, disqualification, and imprisonment subject to the statutory thresholds.
Insolvency, creditor prejudice, and unlawful distributions

Statutory sanction: Consequences may include repayment of unlawful distributions, damages, insolvency clawback, director disqualification, liability for the insolvency deficit, and criminal sanctions for asset concealment or creditor fraud.

Director personal liability: Directors may be personally liable for restitution, creditor compensation, the insolvency deficit, asset seizure, management disqualification, and imprisonment where criminal conduct is proven. Courts may impose precautionary travel restrictions in criminal or insolvency proceedings.
